name: GhostRedirector
iocPatterns: malicious domain names used for payload hosting or C2
SQL injection exploitation in web apps
ZIP/RAR attachments containing malicious LNK scripts
directory traversal to write beyond intended areas
digital signing with unknown third‑party certificates (e.g., SSL.com)
keyCapabilities: Custom privilege escalation utilities (EfsPotato, BadPotato, CVE‑2025-6218/8088 for WinRAR)
Backdoor development (Rungan, Gamshen, Poseidon, MiniJunk, EAGLET)
Malicious IIS module deployment for SEO fraud
Public domain hosting and HTTP-based C&C
SQL injection exploitation in victim web applications
PowerShell or cmd.exe scripts to download additional payloads via certutil.exe
AES‑CBC decryption of encrypted strings within backdoors
Directory traversal to write files outside intended locations
Phishing with ZIP/RAR attachments and LNK payload launchers
DLL injection into Windows Defender using DllPath manipulation
Linux persistence via disguised .desktop files and cron jobs
recommendedActions: Patch all public‑facing web applications and databases to mitigate SQL injection risks.
Deploy a Web Application Firewall (WAF) that blocks malicious HTTP requests targeting PowerShell or cmd.exe payloads.
Monitor outbound DNS queries for known malicious domains used by GhostRedirector for C2 and payload delivery.
Set up network and endpoint monitoring to detect usage of certutil.exe or other downloader utilities as part of lateral movement.
Configure endpoint protection to alert on .NET Reactor obfuscation and unknown DLL injection into system processes.
Restrict use of remote access tools such as GoToHTTP unless absolutely required, and enforce least‑privilege for remote sessions.
Update WinRAR immediately if any version < current patch level is in use, especially addressing CVE‑2025‑6218/CVE‑2025‑8088.
Implement email filtering to block LNK, ZIP, and RAR attachments with executable entries.
Enforce application whitelisting; block untrusted execution of rundll32.exe from non‑trusted sources.
Enable agent‑based monitoring for orphaned cron jobs or suspicious persistence mechanisms on Linux hosts.
Deploy EDR capable of detecting in‑memory .NET payloads and DLL injections into Windows Defender.
Validate all digital signatures; reject executables signed with unverified or third‑party certificates like those from SSL.com.
campaignsText: GhostRedirector’s campaign signatures manifest through repeated usage of IIS malware modules for SEO manipulation, spearphishing attachments that trigger PowerShell or LNK execution, and CVE‑based exploitation of WinRAR to achieve remote shell on Windows hosts. The group leverages a modular toolkit—combining custom backdoors with commercial software—to adapt to various environments, with operations labeled CargoTalon (email delivery), Transparent Tribe/Poseidon (Linux persistence) and Nimbus Manticore (DLL injection into Defender). Across sectors, the actor maintains an asynchronous operational tempo: initial compromise via SQL injection or phishing, followed by lateral movement facilitated by remote access tools such as GoToHTTP and exploitation of unpatched vulnerabilities. Victim types range from state‑owned infrastructure to commercial enterprises, reflecting a broad threat appetite but a shared focus on vulnerable public interfaces.
description: GhostRedirector is a China‑aligned threat actor that compromises Windows servers across a broad spectrum of industries, predominantly in Brazil, Thailand and Vietnam. It deploys custom backdoors such as Rungan and the malicious IIS module Gamshen to maintain persistence while inflating search engine rankings for monetized domains. The group leverages public exploits, privilege escalation utilities like EfsPotato/BadPotato, phishing campaigns, and code‑signing certificates to evade detection and expand lateral movement.
goals: The actor’s primary economic incentive is to monetize through search engine fraud achieved by hijacking IIS modules (Gamshen) to skew indexing for profit. Target selection spans critical national sectors—including telecommunications, financial services, defense, aviation, energy, healthcare, education, retail, and government—and focuses on countries with perceived weaker security postures such as Brazil, Thailand, Vietnam, China, and Ukraine. GhostRedirector’s choice of targets is driven more by the likelihood of successful exploitation (public‑facing applications, unsophisticated security teams) than by any ideological agenda.
